reference.source: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery / Grainger & Allison's Diagnostic Radiology
clinicalPearls: Arises from absence or laxity of the splenic suspensory ligaments (gastrosplenic, splenorenal and phrenocolic), allowing the spleen to migrate on a long, mobile vascular pedicle
May be congenital, from failure of the dorsal mesogastrium to fuse, or acquired through multiparity, hormonally mediated ligamentous laxity or splenomegaly
Typically presents in children and women of reproductive age as a mobile palpable abdominal or pelvic mass, intermittent pain, or an acute abdomen when the pedicle twists
Torsion of the pedicle is the feared complication, producing venous congestion followed by arterial infarction of the spleen
Cross-sectional imaging shows an empty splenic fossa with an ectopically sited spleen; a whirl sign of the twisted pedicle with absent Doppler flow indicates torsion
Splenopexy to fix a viable spleen is preferred, especially in children, to preserve immune function, with splenectomy reserved for a non-viable infarcted organ
May coexist with gastric volvulus, intestinal malrotation and diaphragmatic or abdominal wall defects, reflecting shared abnormal visceral fixation
A palpable notched mass that can be manually returned towards the left upper quadrant is a helpful clinical clue
reference.pathophysiology: The spleen is normally anchored in the left upper quadrant by peritoneal ligaments derived from the dorsal mesogastrium. When these ligaments fail to develop or become lax, the spleen loses its fixation and hangs from an elongated pedicle carrying the splenic vessels, so that it can migrate freely into the abdomen or pelvis. The mobile, narrow pedicle is prone to rotation; torsion first obstructs the thin-walled splenic vein, producing congestion and enlargement, and if it progresses occludes the arterial supply, causing ischaemia and infarction. Chronic partial torsion may instead produce venous congestion with hypersplenism, while the elongated vessels can also compromise the pancreatic tail and predispose to associated gastric volvulus.
additionalDifferentials: Ovarian or other adnexal mass or torsion
Acute appendicitis when the spleen lies in the right or lower abdomen
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, assessing the splenic fossa and the vascular pedicle
Doppler ultrasound of the ectopic spleen to assess perfusion and the twisted pedicle
Technetium sulphur-colloid or heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy to confirm splenic tissue and viability
MRI, favoured in children to limit ionising radiation
Full blood count to detect cytopenias from hypersplenism
Assessment for associated gastric volvulus or malrotation when clinically suspected
redFlags: Acute severe abdominal pain with a tender mobile mass, indicating pedicle torsion
Signs of infarction with peritonism and systemic upset
Haemodynamic instability suggesting infarction with haemorrhage
Retching with inability to pass a nasogastric tube, suggesting associated gastric volvulus
reference.prognosis: When recognised and treated before infarction, splenopexy carries an excellent outcome and preserves splenic immune function. Delayed diagnosis of torsion leads to infarction and loss of the spleen, with the attendant lifelong risks of hyposplenism.
pitfalls: Mistaking the ectopic spleen for a tumour and proceeding to biopsy or inappropriate resection
Delayed recognition of torsion, converting a salvageable spleen into a non-viable one
Performing splenectomy when splenopexy would have preserved function, particularly in children
Omitting post-splenectomy immunisation and antibiotic prophylaxis when the spleen must be removed
management: Perform splenopexy to fix a viable spleen in its normal position, preferred especially in children to preserve immune function
Operate as an emergency on acute pedicle torsion, undertaking detorsion and splenopexy if the spleen is viable
Reserve splenectomy for a non-viable, infarcted spleen or established torsion with infarction
When splenectomy is unavoidable, give pre- and post-splenectomy pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus vaccination with antibiotic prophylaxis against overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
Look for and manage associated gastric volvulus or malrotation at the time of surgery
Monitor the full blood count for cytopenias arising from hypersplenism
Educate patients to seek urgent review for acute abdominal pain suggesting torsion
